idiom_name: abstract record per grammar rule + switch expression with property/type patterns
implementation_notes: Records give compact immutable nodes and one switch expression over type and property patterns gives the evaluator; small grammars fit in a single file and the tree is data. C# 9 has no compiler-enforced exhaustiveness, so keep a throwing discard arm and promote warning CS8509 to an error; C# 15 union types make the same switch exhaustive without the arm. The classic abstract class with a virtual Interpret method remains the shape for a node set that other assemblies must be able to extend.
pitfalls: Without the discard arm a new node record falls through to a compiler warning (CS8509) rather than a build failure; treat warnings as errors in the project file.
Positional record patterns deconstruct by constructor order, so inserting a positional parameter in the middle silently re-binds every pattern that matched that node.
Records are shallowly immutable - a collection-valued child stays mutable - and recursive Eval consumes stack per nesting level.

variants.name: System.Linq.Expressions trees (BCL interpreter)
variants.idiom_name: Expression<Func<T, R>> trees walked by an ExpressionVisitor or compiled with Compile()
variants.implementation_notes: When the interpreted language is an expression language over .NET values, the BCL already ships the pattern: the compiler can turn a lambda into an Expression<Func<T,R>> tree, ExpressionVisitor walks it for translation or optimisation, and Compile() turns it into a delegate - EF Core translates the same trees to SQL instead. Writing node classes by hand is justified only for a grammar the BCL cannot express, and walking an Expression tree beats parsing and interpreting text when the rules are authored in C#.
pitfalls: Compile() emits IL and is expensive per call: compile once, cache the delegate, never inside a loop.
Compiling or interpreting user-supplied expression text is an injection surface; if the source is untrusted, whitelist node types instead of calling Compile().
The tree mirrors C# syntax, so a non-C# rule surface needs its own parser producing Expression nodes - the BCL supplies the evaluator, not the grammar.
